prompt: Compare the two papers imported in this project and identify where they substantively disagree. Support each empirical claim with the passage it comes from.

documents.title: Group Commit in Embedded Stores (Okafor & Lindqvist, 2023)
documents.text:
# Group Commit in Embedded Stores
Okafor, N. and Lindqvist, E. (2023). Proceedings of the Workshop on Embedded Data Systems.

## Method
We modified an embedded SQL store to delay fsync and group all commits arriving within a fixed window. We tested windows of 0, 2, 4 and 8 ms on four enterprise NVMe drives, all with power-loss protection capacitors. The workload was 1 KB inserts from 16 threads.

## Results
An 8 ms window raised throughput by a factor of 3.1 compared with per-transaction fsync. The 99th percentile commit latency rose from 4 ms to 11 ms. In 200 forced power-cut trials we observed no loss of acknowledged transactions at any window size.

## Conclusion
Group commit with an 8 ms window is a safe default for embedded stores: durability is unaffected and throughput triples.

documents.title: Does Group Commit Survive Power Loss? (Marchetti et al., 2024)
documents.text:
# Does Group Commit Survive Power Loss on Consumer Drives?
Marchetti, G., Oyelaran, T. and Brandt, K. (2024). Journal of Practical Storage, 9(3).

## Method
We repeated the group-commit experiment of Okafor and Lindqvist on six consumer SATA solid-state drives whose volatile write caches cannot be disabled. We used the same 1 KB insert workload and windows of 0, 2, 4 and 8 ms, and cut power 500 times per configuration.

## Results
Throughput rose by a factor of 1.4 at an 8 ms window. Tail latency increased, as in the earlier study. With windows longer than 2 ms, up to 0.7% of transactions that had been acknowledged to the client were missing after power was restored. At 2 ms or below we observed no loss.

## Discussion
The earlier claim that durability is unaffected does not generalise. Its drives all had power-loss protection. On consumer hardware we recommend a window of at most 2 ms.

truth: The papers disagree on (1) durability: Okafor & Lindqvist say group commit leaves durability unaffected, Marchetti et al. measure up to 0.7% of acknowledged transactions lost on power failure with windows above 2 ms on consumer SATA drives with volatile write caches; (2) the size of the throughput gain: 3.1x versus 1.4x; (3) the recommended commit window: 8 ms versus no more than 2 ms. They agree that tail latency rises. Marchetti attributes the difference to hardware: Okafor tested only enterprise NVMe drives with power-loss protection. Neither paper reports results for spinning disks or for network storage, and a good answer does not invent any, nor declare one paper simply right beyond what the passages support.
